name: Sermorelin
evidenceNote: Sermorelin was once FDA-approved for children with growth hormone deficiency, but the uses it is sold for now, such as aging, body composition and sleep, rest on small, short studies of a few dozen adults or fewer.
summary: Sermorelin is a short copy of the hormone that tells the pituitary to release growth hormone. Once approved for children, its US approvals were withdrawn in 2009.
keyTakeaway: Sermorelin is the first 29 amino acids of GHRH, the brain hormone that prompts the pituitary to release growth hormone. The FDA approved it as Geref for testing pituitary function in 1990 and for children with growth hormone deficiency in 1997. The maker discontinued both in 2008, and the FDA later confirmed this was not for safety or effectiveness reasons. No sermorelin product is FDA-approved today, though compounding pharmacies and clinics still supply it, mostly for aging. In a 16-week study of 19 older adults, a close analog raised growth hormone and IGF-1 but increased lean mass only in men. It is prohibited in sport.

blocks.text: Sermorelin is a synthetic peptide matching the first 29 amino acids of human growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH), the signal the hypothalamus sends to the pituitary gland to release growth hormone [2].

EMD Serono sold it in the United States as Geref [1]. Today sermorelin is sold through compounding pharmacies with a prescription, through anti-aging and wellness clinics, and through unregulated online sellers, whose products may be contaminated or mislabeled [5].

Sermorelin had two FDA approvals. The first, in December 1990, was a small ampule used as a diagnostic test of whether the pituitary could release growth hormone. The second, in September 1997, was a larger vial for treating idiopathic growth hormone deficiency in children with growth failure [1].

In 2008 EMD Serono told the FDA it was discontinuing both products and asked for the approvals to be withdrawn, which took effect in June 2009. After a 2012 citizen petition, the FDA reviewed its records and concluded in 2013 that Geref had not been withdrawn for reasons of safety or effectiveness. That finding means a generic version could in principle be approved [1]. No other sermorelin product appears in the FDA's approved drug records.

blocks.text: Sermorelin binds GHRH receptors on growth hormone-producing cells in the pituitary and prompts them to release their stores, so growth hormone rises within minutes [2]. Growth hormone then drives the liver to make IGF-1, which carries out many of growth hormone's effects on tissue [3].

Sermorelin is often promoted for sleep, based on the observation that the biggest nightly growth hormone pulse coincides with deep, slow-wave sleep. A 2004 study tested the link in healthy young men by blocking their own GHRH overnight. Growth hormone release was suppressed by 93%, but the share of slow-wave sleep did not change, leading the authors to conclude GHRH is needed for the nighttime growth hormone surge but probably does not generate deep sleep [6].

Not at present. Both Geref approvals were withdrawn in 2009 at the maker's request, and no replacement product has been approved [1]. Sermorelin that is prescribed today comes from compounding pharmacies or from clinics and websites, outside any current FDA approval [5].

The U.S. Anti-Doping Agency lists sermorelin as prohibited in sport because it can boost muscle growth, endurance and recovery, and calls a therapeutic use exemption highly unlikely because better-established treatments for growth hormone deficiency exist [5].

The strongest human data come from its original use in children. A 1999 review found that a single intravenous dose of 1 microgram per kilogram worked as a fairly specific test for growth hormone deficiency, with fewer false positives than other stimulation tests. For treatment, limited data showed nightly injections under the skin raised growth speed in some prepubertal children over 12 months, though the increase was smaller than with injected growth hormone, and the effect on final adult height was never established [2].

Adult data are thin. In a 1997 study, 19 healthy adults aged 55 to 71 injected a close analog of sermorelin, [Nle27]GHRH(1-29), nightly for 16 weeks after a month of placebo. Growth hormone and IGF-1 rose in both sexes and skin got thicker. Lean body mass, insulin sensitivity, well-being and libido improved in men but not in women, and sleep quality did not change in either group [3]. A companion analysis of the same volunteers reported increases in several immune cell types [4].

blocks.text: These adult studies were small, single-blind, short and without a separate placebo group running in parallel. None measured outcomes such as fractures, strength, disability or survival, and none ran long enough to judge long-term risks of raising IGF-1. Side effects in the pediatric data were mostly facial flushing and injection-site pain [2], while the 1997 adult study reported a temporary rise in blood lipids [3].
